fk0: First the ground shook. Then the sea rose.
And then a nuclear plant lost its power.
This is the story of Fukushima.
fk1: The east coast of Japan. On the shore of the Pacific, the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant.
Six reactors. A large share of Tokyo's electricity came from here.
That day, units 1, 2 and 3 were running. Units 4, 5 and 6 were shut for maintenance.
All of unit 4's fuel had been taken out of the reactor and placed in a pool of water.
At the entrance to the nearby town of Futaba stood a sign.
"Nuclear power: energy for a bright future."
fk2: 2:46 in the afternoon. Under the sea, two plates of the earth slipped.
Magnitude 9. The biggest earthquake in Japan's recorded history.
The ground shook for about six minutes.
The plant's reactors shut down automatically. The control rods went in.
Power from outside was cut. Then the emergency diesel generators started.
In the control room, everything was still under control. But the real danger was in the sea.
fk3: About fifty minutes after the earthquake, the sea began to draw back.
Then, one after another, the tsunami waves came.
The plant had been designed for a wave of about six metres.
But the wave that came was fourteen to fifteen metres high.
Water filled the basements of the turbine buildings. That is where the generators stood.
One by one, all the generators stopped.
fk4: The control room went dark. The instruments died.
The reactors were shut down, but the fuel was still giving off tremendous heat.
Keeping it cool needed pumps. And pumps needed electricity.
Workers took batteries out of cars in the car park, so they could read the gauges.
Inside the reactors, the water was boiling away.
fk5: As the water fell, the fuel rods were exposed to the air.
The temperature went above two thousand degrees.
The fuel began to melt. First in unit 1, then in units 2 and 3.
The reaction between hot metal and steam began to make hydrogen gas.
The gas kept collecting under the roof of the reactor building.
fk6: A hydrogen explosion tore through the unit 1 building.
The roof was blown off. Radioactive dust spread into the air.
The evacuation zone kept growing. Two kilometres, then ten, then twenty.
People left with a single bag. They thought it would be a matter of a few days.
fk7: 14 March. An even bigger explosion in unit 3.
15 March. The unit 4 building blew apart too.
Even though its reactor was empty. The hydrogen had come from the next unit, through a pipe.
The same day, unit 2 released the most radiation of all.
The wind was blowing to the north-west. The radiation drifted towards the villages.
fk8: Most of the workers were pulled out.
But some stayed behind. The world called them the Fukushima 50.
They took turns going into the dark buildings, to open valves by hand.
Plant manager Masao Yoshida kept pumping sea water into the reactor, despite orders from above.
He knew the reactor would be ruined for good. But there was no other way.
fk9: 17 March. Army helicopters began dropping sea water from above.
The radiation was so strong they could not stay over the plant for long.
Then came fire engines, and concrete pump trucks with long booms.
The biggest fear was the unit 4 pool. If it dried out, the fuel could catch fire in the open.
Even a plan to evacuate Tokyo had been discussed.
fk10: About one hundred and fifty thousand people had to leave their homes.
Schools, shops, farms. All left just as they were.
Cows and pets wandered the streets.
Poisoned soil was scraped up and packed into black bags. Millions of bags.
In April, Japan rated it level 7. The same as Chernobyl.
fk11: To keep the melted fuel cool, water is still poured in today.
That water becomes radioactive. It was stored in more than a thousand tanks.
To hold back the groundwater, the soil was frozen into a wall of ice.
In 2023, treated water began to be released into the sea.
Robots were sent inside the reactors. Many broke down on the way, ruined by the radiation.
fk12: Just a hundred kilometres away, the Onagawa plant stood on higher ground. It survived.
There had been warnings before. A big tsunami had been predicted years earlier.
After Fukushima, Germany decided to shut down its nuclear plants.
Cleaning up the plant completely will take thirty to forty years.
Chernobyl showed what human error can do.
Fukushima taught that, in front of nature, any wall can turn out to be too small.
